### Part 1 --- Getting started

Who is in the room, how the course works, and then the part that actually matters — turning an interest into a question somebody could answer, and reading enough to know whether somebody already has.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | Aug 26 | **Intro and ideas**<br><span class='goal'>Turn a dataset you did not choose into a question worth asking. Break somebody else's question by naming the filter it fails. Know where to find data you already have.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Three blocks. First, introductions — who I am, and then every one of you: where you are from, what you did before this, your concentration, and what you want out of the program. Second, the course. The arc into AEM 6992, what this is and is not, where the grade goes, and the ground rules for AI — permitted, disclosed, verified, with fabricated citations the one that will bite you. Third, the part that is actually the job: coming up with the question. Five archetypes — evaluation, preference and pricing, prediction and risk, diagnosis, feasibility. For each, what it can claim, what design it needs, and how it fails. Then six anti-patterns, and a filter with four questions.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Where to look first: the Cornell library's holdings and the Dewey marketplace, browsed live. Then the question relay, in groups and against the clock. First your group gets a dataset and writes the best question it can. Then datasets and questions rotate in opposite directions, so you never get your own back. Next you break the question you inherit by naming the filter that kills it, then write your own on a dataset you have not seen. In the last round you may combine any two datasets you have held. Points for questions that survive, and for breaks that land. | One page on what you want to work on and why — before meeting 2 |

### Part 2 --- Evidence, models, and inference

The conceptual core. What a causal claim is, what the standard models estimate, where uncertainty comes from, the difference between explaining and predicting, and how inference goes wrong — taught on examples from industry and the news, before anyone opens a dataset. Teams form in the first meeting of this part.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 2 | Sep 2 | **Causal language**<br><span class='goal'>Draw your project's causal graph. Say which variable you must condition on, and which you must not touch. Leave with your team's ground rules in writing.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Counterfactuals and potential outcomes. Every comparison is a claim about a world that did not happen. Then causal graphs: confounders, colliders, mediators, back-door reasoning. And why controlling for everything makes things worse. Finally the map for the rest of this half. Every design we meet closes a back door in a different way. You will draw each one before you hear what it is called.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> First, teams. You are put into one, and it writes down its own ground rules today, while everybody still gets along. Who does what. What happens when somebody misses a deadline. How you settle a disagreement. One page, signed, handed in. Then your team's first job together. Each team draws a card carrying a real causal claim somebody is acting on — a board paper, a marketing deck, a widely shared post. Every card is broken differently. Draw the graph behind it, then name the failure in this morning's vocabulary. Then one team is drawn at random to defend its diagnosis while the room attacks, and we draw again as the clock allows. You will not know whether you are up. Card 3 is a collider and card 5 is a mediator. Those two are where the morning either landed or it did not. | Your team's written ground rules — agreed and handed in today |
| 3 | Sep 9 | **Models and uncertainty**<br><span class='goal'>Read a coefficient in the units of the problem. Say what a p-value does and does not tell you. Tell an explanatory question apart from a predictive one.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Linear regression, non-linear models, count models. Described, not derived. What each estimates, and how to read a coefficient in the units of the problem. Then uncertainty. Residuals and errors, sampling variation, what a standard error actually states, and where p-values come from. More usefully: what they are not. Finally the distinction that decides half the projects in this room. Explaining is not predicting. A model can predict well and still tell you nothing about what to do.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Ten minutes of simulation first, driven from the front. Draw from a world you control. Watch the p-value distribution under the null. Move the sample size and the variation, and watch it shift. Then fit the same world in and out of sample, and watch an excellent-looking model fail on data it has not seen. Nothing to install. Then the cards. Each team gets an analyst who ran something and said something about it, and every one overclaims differently. A count outcome fitted by OLS and predicted below zero. A 0.03% lift called highly significant across two million users. A wide interval called no effect. An elasticity estimated off two price changes in three years. A churn probability of 112%. Work out what they are actually entitled to claim. Then a team is drawn at random to defend that while the room pushes back. The last line on the sheet is the one that matters: is your own project at risk of the same error? | — |
| 4 | Sep 16 | **How inference fails**<br><span class='goal'>Take a published claim apart. Name the specific failure. Say which direction it pushes the estimate, and whether more data would fix it.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Bias first. Omitted variables, sorting and selection, measurement error — classical and not — and reverse causality. For each: what it does to the estimate, and in which direction. Then false precision, which is the quieter problem. Dependence ignored. Multiple testing. Specification search. The number stays where it is and the error bar shrinks around it.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> First, together: one published claim, taken apart. Which failure is doing the damage? Would more data fix it? Then the same move on a paper from your own literature. Write down the one threat your design will have to survive. You will be answering it in November. | — |
| 5 | Sep 23\* | **Controls and matching**<br><span class='goal'>Draw the back doors a set of controls closes. State exactly what would have to be true for your coefficient to be read causally.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> We start where every design meeting from here starts. At the graph. Conditioning on observables, drawn: which back doors a set of controls closes, and the one you cannot see well enough to close. Then controls and matching in practice, and when a regression coefficient can be read causally. 'I added controls' is a claim about the graph, not a technique. The rest of the session is what would have to be true for that claim to hold.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Back to the graph you drew in meeting 2. Could you close every back door with data you could actually obtain? Breakout rooms, then report back. | — |

### Part 3 --- Research designs

The ways applied economists get a credible estimate, from conditioning on observables to designs built on found variation — what variation each exploits, what each assumes, and how each fails.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 6 | Sep 30 | **Research designs I**<br><span class='goal'>Draw the graph for an experiment, an instrument and a discontinuity. Say whether any of the three is open to your question.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Three designs, each drawn before it is described. Experiments first. Randomisation cuts every arrow into treatment, so there is no back door left to close. Then the decisions that actually make one work. What is the unit you randomise — the person, the store, the week? How many arms can you afford before each one is too thin? Why you check balance afterwards, and what a failure would mean. And pre-registration, the cheapest honesty device in research: say what you will test before you look, and specification search stops being available to you. Instrumental variables next. An arrow into treatment, and none into the outcome except through it. The exclusion restriction is that missing arrow, which is why it cannot be tested. Then regression discontinuity: nothing else jumps at the cutoff. For each, what variation it exploits, what it assumes, how it fails, and what it looks like done well.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Each team draws a setting nobody in the room owns. A bank with an email list. A scholarship cutoff. An NGO that gave filters to whoever asked. Fifteen minutes to draw the graph, name a design, and state the assumption carrying it. Then teams are drawn at random to defend for four minutes while the room attacks. What breaks this? Nobody knows in advance whether they are up. One card cannot be answered honestly at all, and the team holding it has to be willing to say so. Last: is an experiment, an instrument or a discontinuity actually open to your own project? Most teams find the answer is no. Finding that out today rather than in November is the point. | — |
| 7 | Oct 7 | **Research designs II**<br><span class='goal'>Draw your project's design as a graph. Name the single assumption carrying the estimate — the one you would have to defend to a sceptic.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> The same discipline on harder designs, each drawn first. Difference-in-differences: the confounders you cannot measure are the ones that do not move. Parallel trends is what that assumption looks like drawn. Panel data with local fixed effects: which arrows the fixed effects erase, and which survive untouched. Event studies: the same picture with time on it. For each, what identifying variation is left once the fixed effects are in, and what assumption is carrying the estimate.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Same format, higher stakes. First a card apiece — a staggered rollout, a state border, a fee that changed for accounts opened after a date. Fifteen minutes to draw it and name the design. Then the part that counts. Teams are drawn at random to put up their own project's design, draw the graph, state the assumption carrying the estimate, and defend it while the room tries to break it. Everyone presents eventually. Nobody knows when. Whatever survives is the figure that goes in your identification section, so draw it to keep. And write down the attack that landed. That is your limitations paragraph. | — |

### Part 4 --- Communicating the work

Half of what you are graded on is whether somebody else can follow the argument. So it is taught, not assumed. One meeting on writing, one on figures and talking — and in both, session B works on your own project rather than an exercise. The pitch comes out of this part, and so does the method you will use to build the outline in November.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 8 | Oct 14 | **Writing**<br><span class='goal'>Reconstruct the outline behind somebody else's paper. Build your own problem statement the same way, topic sentence by topic sentence, and hand it to a stranger who can follow it.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> The method. A paper is built outline first: one topic sentence per paragraph, in order, before any prose exists. We start backwards — take a published paper apart into the outline that must have produced it. That is also this week's exercise, and the fastest way to see that good writing has a skeleton. Then forwards: outline, sketch, full text. Every written product in this course is submitted that way, so the argument is fixed before the sentences are. Then what a problem statement has to do. Scope, unit, population. The 'so what' in the first sentence, not the fourth paragraph. Then the section everybody gets wrong — identification: your design named, its assumption stated, and what would break it. And how to state a limitation without gutting your own project. Finally the failure modes: the topic with no question, hedging, the buried claim, the review that reviews without arguing.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Your own problem statement, written in the room. One topic sentence per paragraph, in order, and nothing else — no prose. Then swap with another team. They get your skeleton and nothing else, and they have to tell you what your argument is. Where they cannot, your argument is not there yet. Whatever survives that is the spine of your pitch next week, and of the proposal outline in November. | — |
| 9 | Oct 21\* | **Oral and visual**<br><span class='goal'>Name the trick in a figure built to mislead you, and redraw it honestly without losing the point. Then pitch your project in five minutes, on slides where every title is a claim.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Two halves. First, figures. Which figure answers which question, and why — distributions, time, space. The instinct to be curious about a dataset before you model it. Then the flip side: what figures hide through aggregation, scale, binning, projection and cherry-picked windows, and how to read a published figure for what it is not showing. Second, talking. A deck is an outline with pictures. One claim per slide, and the claim is the slide title, not a label. No bullet lists. What the first thirty seconds have to do, what the last thirty have to do, and what to do with a question you cannot answer — which is to say so.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Six figures, each lying a different way, one per team. A truncated axis. Two axes manufacturing a correlation. A cherry-picked window. An aggregate moving opposite to every subgroup. Area scaled by radius. Counts where you needed a rate. Name the trick, then redraw it honestly — and the honest version still has to make a point, which is the hard half nobody practises. Then the pitch. Five minutes per team, five slides, one topic sentence per slide, using the skeleton you wrote last week. The room's questions are aimed at where the argument jumps. Then you rate your teammates for the first time. | Project pitch — one page, presented in class · Writing 1 — reverse outline · Rate your teammates |

### Part 5 --- Measurement, data, and getting hold of it

The step most projects skip. Turning a construct into something a dataset can hold, working out what the design actually demands, and then the practical business of obtaining it — sources, proprietary access, data-use agreements, the IRB, and what scraping and APIs can and cannot get you.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 10 | Oct 28 | **Measurement and data**<br><span class='goal'>Turn your central construct into a variable somebody could record. Specify what the design demands of the data. If nothing measures it, write the instrument that would — and say how many observations it needs to be worth fielding.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Constructs and operationalisation. How do you turn 'sustainability', 'financial literacy' or 'market power' into a variable somebody could actually record? What makes that measure defensible, and what does a proxy cost you? Then work backwards from the design to its data requirements. Unit of observation. Level of aggregation. Time frequency, span, coverage. Which comparisons the data has to contain. Can this be done with county data, or does it need individuals? Finally, the short version of what to ask any dataset before trusting it: what is one row, how many are there, what is missing, what changed over time. The full checklist is on the resources page. You put it to work on real data in meeting 12.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Sometimes nothing measures your construct. Then you make the measurement yourself. Each team gets a real survey item, broken a different way. Leading. Double-barrelled. An unbalanced scale with no way to disagree. A question that assumes you already do the thing. A hypothetical willingness-to-pay that everybody overstates. Name the flaw, rewrite it, and say what an answer to your version would actually let you conclude. Random rotation, room attacks. Then build your own — the instrument your project needs, whether that is survey items, a choice task, or a simple experiment with a treatment and a control. Then work out how many people it needs. The smallest effect you can detect is roughly four sigma over root n. Quadrupling the sample only halves it. So: with the sample you can afford, is the smallest detectable effect still interesting? If not, you have learned that in October rather than March. | Writing 2 — reverse outline and repair |
| 11 | Nov 4 | **Getting the data**<br><span class='goal'>Say what a scraper and an API each are, and when either is the wrong answer. Name your own data source, its access route, its timeline and your plan B — including whether you need IRB approval or a data-use agreement before January.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> First, code. Not how to write it — what it is, and why you cannot avoid understanding it. What a language actually is, and why there are several. R grew out of statistics. Python out of general programming. Stata out of applied economics. SQL is not really the same kind of thing at all. Then the argument that matters here. Every serious analysis is code, whether or not you wrote it. A spreadsheet stops being enough at exactly the point your project gets interesting. And code is the only version of an analysis that can be checked, repeated, and handed to somebody else. You will drive it through an assistant. But you cannot check what you cannot read at all. Then the landscape of sources: administrative records, official statistics, firm and platform data, purchased panels. What each costs in money and in months, starting with what Cornell already pays for. Proprietary access and data-use agreements: who signs, how long, and what they forbid you from publishing. Ethics and the IRB in brief, with the detail on the resources page. Then scraping and APIs: what each is, what it can and cannot get you, and what the terms of service and the law actually say.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> A scrape, run live from the front, then broken on purpose. We pull a table off a page. Then we watch every way it fails. The page changes and the code returns nothing. The rate limit bites. Records go missing and nothing tells you. The terms of service say no. And nothing you pulled could be reproduced by anybody next week. Then the same data through a proper API. Then the same data simply downloaded, which is usually faster than either. The lesson is not that scraping is bad. It is the last resort dressed up as the clever one. Then the acquisition clinic on your own project. Which source, exactly. What route. How long. What it costs. What plan B is. Your memo outline — six topic sentences — comes out of that, and it is due before the weekend. | — |
| 12 | Nov 11 | **Using data**<br><span class='goal'>Say which AI modality suits which job, and why. Interrogate a real dataset through one, and catch something wrong with it before it reaches your proposal.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> First, the modalities. 'Use AI' is four different things. Chat answers from memory, and will invent a citation. File upload with code execution writes and runs real code on your data, so the output is checkable. Retrieval answers from documents you supplied. Agents act over several steps, and compound a mistake made early. The one you want here is the second, and knowing why is the point. Then the harder half, which is the whole skill in this course: knowing whether an answer is right without reading the code that produced it. Row counts across a join. Totals checked against a published figure. Five raw records read by hand. Orders of magnitude. And what you must not upload, and why.<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Real data in front of you, and the meeting-9 checklist put to work: what is one row, how many are there, what is missing, what changed over time. Every dataset handed out has something wrong with it. Find it, then say which check would have caught it — that second half is the graded one. Then the same move on your own project's data. Whatever you cannot answer about it today is what you chase before the outline is due. | Proposal outline · Writing 3 — plain-language summary · Exercise 1 — interrogate a dataset, end of week |
